entities.summary:
Domenico Grimani (1461–1523) was a Venetian nobleman, cardinal, and one of the most prominent ecclesiastical figures and humanists of the Italian Renaissance. Born into the powerful Grimani family, he leveraged his lineage and intellectual prowess to ascend the Church hierarchy, becoming a significant patron of arts and letters and a formidable collector whose library and antiquities rivaled those of popes and princes. His career epitomized the intersection of political power, religious authority, and cultural flourishing characteristic of late 15th and early 16th-century Italy, deeply influencing Venetian intellectual life and the broader European humanist movement.

Grimani's ascent began with his appointment as Patriarch of Aquileia in 1497, a crucial position for Venetian influence in the Adriatic, which he held until his death. Pope Alexander VI elevated him to cardinal in 1503, after which he accumulated immense wealth and influence through the practice of ecclesiastical pluralism, holding numerous bishoprics and abbacies across Italy. He actively participated in several papal conclaves, including those that elected Julius II (1503) and Leo X (1513), demonstrating his political acumen. He also served as a diplomat for the Venetian Republic, navigating the complex political landscape of the Italian Wars, notably mediating between Venice and the Papacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Domenico Grimani's vast library and art collection, bequeathed to the Republic of Venice, formed a crucial foundation for the Biblioteca Marciana and deeply influenced Venetian Renaissance culture. His career as a cardinal and diplomat also underscored the intersection of religious, political, and cultural power in early 16th-century Italy.
